title.zh: 明清（至鸦片战争前）：统一多民族国家的巩固与发展

clips.send: Gate of Divine Prowess. The north gate. In the Ming it was called Xuanwu Gate; in the Qing it was renamed to avoid the Kangxi Emperor’s personal name (Xuanye). Today it is the north exit of the Palace Museum. South gate Wumen in, north gate Shenwumen out.

clips.send: Northeast: Russia invaded the Heilongjiang region. In the Battles of Yaksa (1685–1686) the Qing army defeated them. The Treaty of Nerchinsk (1689) confirmed in law that the Heilongjiang and Ussuri basins, including Sakhalin, were Chinese territory.

clips.send: Ili. Today: Yining and Huocheng, Xinjiang. From Huiyuan city in the green Ili valley, the General of Ili governed all of Xinjiang, including the lands round Lake Balkhash.

clips.send: Common mix-up: Zheng He’s first voyage (1405) was 87 years before Columbus (1492): “more than half a century earlier than the European navigators”.

clips.send: Corner towers. Watchtowers at the four corners of the wall. Each corner of the palace wall has an elaborate tower with many intersecting roofs. A moat 52 metres (170 ft) wide surrounds the wall. Four corners, four towers.

clips.send: Masts and sails. Powered by the monsoon. The treasure ship had many masts with battened sails. The fleet used the monsoon: it usually set out in winter with the northeast monsoon and returned in summer with the southwest monsoon. Winter wind out, summer wind home.

clips.send: Gifts and trade goods. Porcelain and silk went out; spices came back. The fleet brought porcelain (fine “china” dishes), silk, tea and copper coins as gifts and for trade. It brought back spices, jewels, medicines and rare animals. It visited more than 30 countries and regions in Asia and Africa and strengthened China’s friendly ties with them. Peaceful voyages: gifts and trade, not conquest.

clips.send: Halls of Central and Preserving Harmony. The second and third great halls. The Hall of Central Harmony is a small square hall where the emperor rested before ceremonies. In the Qing, the final round of the imperial exams (the tests that chose government officials) was held in the Hall of Preserving Harmony, with the emperor as examiner. Three halls share one terrace.

clips.send: From Calicut the fleet reached Hormuz on the Persian Gulf, Aden and Mecca on the Red Sea coast, and Mogadishu and Malindi on the east coast of Africa, the farthest points of the voyages.

clips.send: The fleet. Dozens of big ships sailing together. Besides treasure ships, the fleet had ships carrying horses, grain, water and soldiers. At sea the ships signalled with flags by day and lanterns by night. Press “ Fleet” to show or hide the other ships. Big fleet equals strong Ming state.

clips.send: Across the Bay of Bengal to Ceylon (Sri Lanka), then to Calicut on India’s southwest coast, a hub where the fleet split up.

clips.send: Southwest: the Qing granted titles to the Dalai Lama (1653) and the Panchen Lama (1713); in 1727 Yongzheng set up the Grand Minister Resident in Tibet; Qianlong created the golden urn lottery for choosing reincarnations. By the mid-18th century the Qing held a vast, unified territory.

clips.send: Meridian Gate (Wumen). The main (south) gate of the Forbidden City. Its U-shaped plan wraps around a courtyard, with towers on both wings. Important ceremonies were held here, such as announcing the new calendar. Wu equals south: the palace faces south.

clips.send: Compass and star-sighting. Advanced navigation technology. The navigators followed compass bearings recorded as “needle routes”. At night they measured the height of stars with sighting boards (牵星板 qiānxīng bǎn) to work out how far north or south they were. Advanced shipbuilding and navigation were key conditions for the voyages. Compass by day and night, stars to find the place.

clips.send: Central axis. Everything lines up north–south. The main buildings lie on one north–south central axis, with the others arranged symmetrically on both sides. The layout shows the supreme power of the emperor. In 2024 the Beijing Central Axis joined the UNESCO World Heritage List. Toggle the glowing axis, then walk it with the story!

clips.send: To strengthen ties with overseas countries, the Yongle Emperor sent Zheng He to the “Western Oceans”. In 1405 the great fleet left Liujiagang. From 1405 to 1433 he made seven voyages.

clips.send: Kuye Island. Today: Sakhalin, Russia. A long, cold island north of Japan. The Treaty of Nerchinsk counted it as Chinese land, but Russia seized it in the 19th century.
clips.text: Kuye Island. Today: Sakhalin, Russia. A long, cold island north of Japan. The Treaty of Nerchinsk counted it as Chinese land, but Russia seized it in the 19th century.

clips.send: The Forbidden City. Built under the Yongle Emperor of the Ming: planned from 1406 and basically finished in 1420; the capital moved to Beijing in 1421. That is 72 years before Columbus sailed. The palace of 24 Ming and Qing emperors; today the Palace Museum. The largest and best-preserved ancient palace complex in the world (World Heritage, 1987): about 72 hectares (178 acres), roughly 135 football fields.

clips.send: Northwest: Kangxi defeated Galdan of the Dzungars; Qianlong put down the Dzungar rebellion and the revolt of the Greater and Lesser Khojas, and in 1762 set up the General of Ili to govern Xinjiang. In 1771 the Torghut Mongols returned from the Volga.

clips.send: Treasure ship. Flagship of the Ming fleet. From 1405 to 1433 Zheng He (郑和 Zhèng Hé) led a fleet to the “Western Oceans” (the seas west of the South China Sea) seven times. The History of Ming records that the largest treasure ships were 44 zhang long and 18 zhang wide (a zhang 丈 is an old unit of about 10 feet), which would make them longer than a football field. Historians still debate the exact size, but they were among the largest wooden ships of the age. Columbus’s flagship in 1492 was only about 60 ft (19 m) long. The fleet carried more than 20,000 people, as many as a small town, and set out from Liujiagang (in Taicang, Jiangsu Province, near today’s Shanghai). Zheng He: 1405–1433, seven voyages, 30+ countries, farthest to East Africa and the Red Sea.

clips.send: Nerchinsk. Today: Nerchinsk, Russia. In 1689 China and Russia signed a treaty here that fixed the eastern part of their border along the Argun River and the Outer Khingan Mountains.

clips.send: Volga River. Today: Russia. Europe’s longest river. In 1771 the Torghut people under Ubashi set out from here and trekked thousands of kilometres east to return to China.
clips.text: Volga River. Today: Russia. Europe’s longest river. In 1771 the Torghut people under Ubashi set out from here and trekked thousands of kilometres east to return to China.

clips.send: Common mix-up: Zheng He reached “the east coast of Africa and the Red Sea coast” at the farthest, not Europe or the Americas. The “Western Oceans” meant the seas and coasts west of the South China Sea. He sailed in the Ming (1405–1433), not the Yuan or Qing.

clips.send: Yaksa. Today: Albazino, Russia. Russian forces built a fort here on the Heilongjiang. Kangxi’s army besieged it twice and won; then the two sides signed the Treaty of Nerchinsk.

clips.send: Hall of Supreme Harmony. The largest hall: grand ceremonies. It stands on a three-tier white marble terrace and has the highest-ranking double-eaved hip roof. Emperors held their enthronement, weddings and other grand ceremonies here. The Forbidden City was the palace of both the Ming and Qing dynasties. Front court: “Tai–Zhong–Bao” (Supreme, Central, Preserving Harmony).

clips.send: Through the Strait of Malacca: Malacca became a base where the fleet stored goods; nearby Samudra (Sumatra) and Java were also visited.

clips.send: Zheng He visited more than 30 countries and regions in Asia and Africa. The voyages strengthened China’s friendly exchange with them. They were a feat in world navigation, more than half a century earlier than the European voyages.

clips.send: The fleet sailed south along the coast to Changle in Fujian to wait for the winter monsoon, then crossed the South China Sea to Champa (today’s Vietnam).

clips.send: Inner Court: the three rear palaces. Where the emperor lived and worked. Palace of Heavenly Purity, Hall of Union, Palace of Earthly Tranquillity. The front court (outer) was for ceremonies; the inner court was for daily life and routine government. Front for ceremony, back for living: “front court, rear palaces”.

clips.send: Now to the Qing (map of China). In 1662 Zheng Chenggong drove out the Dutch colonists and recovered Taiwan. In 1684 the Qing set up Taiwan Prefecture under Fujian Province. (Earlier, in the Ming, Qi Jiguang had defeated the pirates on the southeast coast.)

clips.send: 罗盘与牵星术。先进的航海技术。航海人员用罗盘确定方向，并记录成“针路”。夜间用“牵星板”测量星辰的高度来确定船的位置，叫“过洋牵星术”。先进的造船和航海技术是郑和下西洋的重要条件。罗盘定方向，牵星定位置。

clips.send: 中轴线。建筑沿南北中轴线排列。主要建筑都排列在一条南北中轴线上，其他建筑左右对称分布。这种布局体现了皇权至高无上。2024年，“北京中轴线”被列入《世界遗产名录》。打开发光的中轴线，再用“故事”沿着它走一遍！

clips.text: 紫禁城。明成祖时修建：1406年开始筹建，1420年基本建成，1421年迁都北京。。明清两代共24位皇帝在这里居住和处理政务，今为故宫博物院。。世界上现存规模最大、保存最完整的古代宫殿建筑群（1987年列入《世界遗产名录》）。

clips.send: 库页岛。今天：俄罗斯萨哈林岛。日本北面一座狭长寒冷的大岛。《尼布楚条约》肯定它属于中国，19世纪被沙俄侵占。

clips.send: 郑和访问了亚非三十多个国家和地区，加强了中国同亚非各国的友好往来和经济文化交流。郑和下西洋是世界航海史上的壮举，比欧洲航海家的远航早半个多世纪。

clips.send: 易错点：郑和下西洋“最远到达非洲东海岸和红海沿岸”，并没有到达欧洲或美洲；“西洋”指今天的南海以西的海洋和沿岸地区。郑和是明朝人（1405—1433年），不是元朝或清朝。

clips.send: 太和殿。紫禁城中最大的宫殿。建在三层汉白玉台基上，屋顶是等级最高的重檐庑殿顶。皇帝登基、大婚等重大典礼在这里举行。紫禁城是明清两代的皇宫。外朝三大殿：太和、中和、保和。

clips.send: 郑和宝船。明朝船队的主力大船。1405年至1433年，郑和先后七次率领船队下西洋。据《明史》记载，大的宝船长四十四丈、宽十八丈，是当时世界上最大的木帆船之一。船队人员有两万多人，从刘家港（今江苏太仓）出发。郑和下西洋：1405—1433，七次，三十多个国家，最远到非洲东海岸和红海沿岸。
